concept.name: Market fragmentation
concept.definition: The dispersion of trading in the same instrument across multiple competing venues — exchanges, ECNs, dark pools, and internalizing broker-dealers — rather than concentration in a single marketplace. The SEC has described current U.S. equity market structure as dispersed and complex, with volume spread among many automated trading centers.
concept.intuition: The same stock trades in a dozen different rooms at once; no single room sees all the buyers and sellers.
concept.mechanics: Competing venues attract order flow with fees, speed, and order types; linkage rules (Regulation NMS order protection, consolidated data) stitch quotes together, so smart order routers must sweep many venues to assemble liquidity that would once have pooled in one book.
concept.failure_modes: Fragmentation can inhibit interaction of investor orders and impair efficiency and best execution; it also complicates surveillance, since no single venue sees the complete order flow in a security.
concept.misconceptions: Fragmentation is not purely a defect — the SEC weighs it against the benefits of competition among markets (lower fees, innovation); consolidation into one venue would create a monopoly.
concept.example: A single NYSE-listed stock trades simultaneously on NYSE, Nasdaq, Cboe, dozens of ATSs, and inside broker-dealers, with the listing exchange executing well under half of consolidated volume.

citations.source: SEC, Concept Release on Equity Market Structure (Release No. 34-61358)
citations.section: Sections I-II (dispersed market structure; fragmentation vs. competition)
